Penny for your thoughts - Scoin

By: Graham Coetzer | Production

Proposal


Show: Carte Blanche

One Liner (Tonight on Carte Blanche...):
Our investigation reveals how the group of Scoin shops across the country are grossly misleading the public on so called great investment coins

Unique Selling Point:
Our hidden camera footage reveals how brokers at three of the Scoin shops in Johannesburg blatantly mislead would be investors into believing that 1. They will have huge returns on investment if the buy collectable/commemorative coins, and that they 2. sell said coins at grossly over inflated prices and 3. that they promise to buy back the coins after a suitable period ie 5 years. Our case studies have all bought coins under the same sales pitch, and none of them have seen any return on investment. In fact they've all lost on their initial capital input and the coins are worth little more then the value of the precious metals they contain. A second hidden camera investigation where we accompanied a case study to Scoin's head office in Sandton shows a senior sales executive explaining to the case study that his coins are worth nowhere near what he paid for them and that despite years having passed they are now worth nothing more then the precious metals they contain, and also that despite their promises Scoin will not buy back the coins from them. It also shows a sales broker telling the case study that the he doesn't want to see him "get burned again" on the new platinum kruger rands that Scoin tried to sell us in the first hidden camera footage at the various shops.

Summary:
Scoin is misleading gullible buyers into spending hundreds of thousands of rands on coins they punt as investments, that will never realise anywhere near the price that the public is paying for them. They are doing so knowingly, and despite numerous complaints on social media, radio stations etc the continue to operate with impunity. Our hidden camera footage, and the experts we will speak to, prove beyond doubt that this is nothing more than a cleverly packaged scam.

Peter Lycklama
Rohini Shookan
Gavin Lightfoot

Script:


Voice
In tough economic times growing your personal wealth is a tricky business. One way of doing that is by investing your money on the stock market – but some people prefer alternative assets such as gold bullion or even rare coins. (12.24)
Link John
Would you part with hundreds of thousands of rands of your hard earned cash as an investment in rare coins on the advice of a salesman? Well we’ve received dozens of complaints from people who did precisely that only to find that far from making a return, they actually lost money.
Voice
Our case studies said they were disappointed by promises made to them by coin dealers Scoin. So we decided to visit a few of their shops in the Johannesburg area with our hidden cameras. First stop – their Sandton City Branch. We told the salesmen we had a R100 000 to invest, and they suggested we buy what they called rare and collectable coins. (19.21)
Sound Up Hiddencam
Your rare collectable coins, like your proof coins, would be more your long term investment.
Voice
They offered some examples of the growth they said our investment could achieve.(5.07)
Sound Up Hiddencam
Salesman: Your 2014 proof set, came out with all the decimals, one ounce, half ounce, quarter ounce and one tenth. It came out at R44 000 in 2014. It’s now R75 000.
Voice
They also said that if we kept the coins for at least 5 to 7 years, they would buy them back from us.(5.02)
Sound Up Hiddencam
CB Investigator: But you will take it back?
Salesman: Ja. The longer you hold onto it…
CB Investigator: The better?
Salesman: The better. What you need to look for…
CB Investigator: So it’s quite safe? Because that’s a key thing to me. I don’t know anyone in the coin industry so how do I sell them again in 10 years time?
Salesman: We’ve been around for 40 odd years.
CB Investigator: So you’ll definitely take… Is that an agreement is it on paper or…
Salesman: We can, we can do something.
Voice 
They suggested we buy two 1oz Proof Platinum Kruger Rands at a cool R45 000 each. The difference between a Proof Kruger and a regular Kruger is essentially cosmetic. A proof Kruger is struck twice so the image that appears on it is more defined and it is frosted to give it a brighter exterior. The value of their precious metal is exactly the same. So if you had gold Krugers and you wanted to sell your gold you would get paid exactly the same for your proof coin as your bullion coin. (29.14)
Sound Up Hiddencam
Salesman: That’s your certificate of authenticity. And that’s the coin.
CB Investigator: It feels heavier than you would think.
Salesman: It’s encapsulated so that you can handle it.
Voice 
The coin contains 1 ounce of platinum, which at today’s prices is worth roughly R12,200. That’s much less than the R45 000 price tag Scoin is selling it for. But the salesman assured us it was a rare collectible and that we could expect very good returns on it.(11.00)
Sound Up Hiddencam
CB Investigator: Ten years down the line, what’s it going to be worth?
Salesman: You’ll definitely double it. You’ll definitely double it in less than that.
Voice
It is pure speculation whether the coin would ever achieve that kind of growth, but according to our case studies Scoin’s promises did not materialize for them. Peter Lucyklama bought his first coins and gold medallions from Scoin in 2011 and 2012, spending R98 500. (17.09)
Sound Up Peter Lycklama
They say that at least you are looking at 300 or 400% value in a five year, ok, that it will increase in value.
Voice
Lycklama says after the 5 year period had expired and he wanted to sell his coins back to Scoin, they declined to purchase some of them and offered him less than he had paid for the rest.(9:13)
Sound Up Peter
Why must I try and sell the coin at a loss?
Voice
At the Scoin shop in Cresta we were again assured the rare collectibles would increase in value over 5 to 7 years.(6:17)
Sound Up Hiddencam
Salesman: Rare collectibles you have to keep for a minimum of 5 to 7 years, it will obviously increase in value.
Voice
And the growth forecast on some of the coins sounded great(3:18)
Sound Up Hiddencam
Salesman: I’d say it will probably jump up by another R50 000 hey, in the next year or two.
CB Investigator: Really? Fifty grand more?
Salesman: Definitely.
Voice
And they also promised to buy them back from us.(3:10)
Sound Up Hiddencam
CB Investigator: The rare collectibles, let’s say I keep them 5 years, 10 years, who do I sell them to?
Salesman 1: Back to us.
Salesman 2: We do offer a buy back policy. But you can also sell it privately.

Voice
Ex-motorcycling champion Gavin Lightfoot says he was looking at investing money from a retirement annuity when a friend told him about the Scoin shops.(8:09)
Sound Up Gavin
Well I had a R.A., which with some savings that I put into it, I put in just over R800 000.
Voice
And like Peter, Gavin says the promised returns sounded too good to refuse.(4:12)
Sound Up Gavin
They showed me the growth you know of the various coins, and how they’d escalated in value over the years. So it looked like a promising investment, and that’s why I went with it.
Voice
Rohini Shookan also invested a significant amount based on Scoin’s sales pitch of both growth and a buyback.(8:01)
Sound Up Rohini
John: Rohini, why exactly did you decide to invest in coins?
Rohini: I was told that it’s a very good investment opportunity, I have to keep the coins for five to seven years, and after five to seven years the value would have grown quite significantly. And it would be able to be sold on the open market or Scoin would be able to buy it back.
Voice
But after waiting the prescribed period of time, Shookan says she had trouble selling them back to Scoin.(6:01)
Sound Up Rohini
I even met, I think it’s the head of the customer services Kevin, to have the discussion with him and said this is my portfolio can you buy it back? And he says no he’s not willing to buy it back. There are two or three coins that he will buy back but it will be close to the purchase price that I paid.
Voice
Gavin received regular updates from Scoin, which showed how his coins had appreciated in value.(5:23)

Sound Up Gavin
My biggest problem was that even after two years when I approached them to buy back when they’d updated my portfolio, and it had actually realized a gain, they weren’t prepared to buy the coins back. So even if I wanted to sell them back after two years, based on their information and how it had increased in value, they weren’t prepared to buy them back so.
Voice
There are 25 Scoin shops nationwide, and this man, Alan Demby, owns them all. He says Scoin customers need to do their research and consider their coins as long term investments.(10:07)
Sound Up Alan Demby:
Alan: Well, those people who bought the coins with the intention of selling are not collectors, they are not even investors, they are speculators.
Voice
Demby says between 2004 and 2013 they bought back millions of rands in coins, and will do so once again as soon as the markets recover.(9:05)
Link John
We all know that rare coins are extremely collectible, their value is determined by their precious metal content, their condition and their scarcity. But collect-ability isn’t something that can be manufactured.
Sound Up Alan Demby
Alan: And the market may well pick up again.
John: You see this is where we have a difficulty. Because what you are doing there Alan is you are manufacturing a value. You are manufacturing rarity. You are manufacturing desirability. On the basis that there is something that you consider significant happening next year, other people would disagree. And that down the line those medallions are going to be worth something. You have no way of saying that?
Alan: Nobody has. In 1997-
John: But you’ll manufacture the interest anyway, and you’ll get people to buy those coins?
Alan: People love Mandela. People love democracy.
John: I’m afraid that’s not a good enough answer Alan. You are asking people to part with their hard earned money on the basis of a pipe dream. It doesn’t matter that they love Mandela. So do I, but I wouldn’t buy a coin for R145 000.
John: You don’t have to. But there are some people who spend R10million on a coin. The difference is that those are people who have done their research. And if you pay a R145 000 and you have not found out, and you have not done your research, you may well be unhappy.
Voice
We spoke to one of South Africa’s leading coin specialists Glen Schoeman who is also the chairman of the South African Association of Numismatic Dealers. (8:21)
Sound Up Glen Schoeman
If you bought something from a particular dealer, and that particular dealer is not prepared to give you a reasonable amount of money back for it, you’ve got to understand that you were probably overcharged in the first place. If it was such a good investment he would be glad to buy it back from you because he can then sell it on to the next client and make a profit from it again.
Voice
Demby sites a 10 years of democracy coin as a perfect example of how coins grow in value.(6:00)
Sound Up Alan
Well actually the South African Mint, they minted a tenth anniversary coin, which we sold. In fact we sold it for R4000 and today they are trading at about R60 000.
Voice
A quick Google search shows that a Mandela 10 years of democracy coin that Scoin sells for R60 000 can be bought from other dealers for R19 000.(9:13)
Sound Up Glen
John: Have you received any calls from people wanting to buy the 10 years of democracy coin?
Glen: What we do get is people sending us lists, and that item does appear on the list that they are wanting to sell that we’ve had a lot of. But we haven’t had people coming and asking us that they want to buy them from us no.
Voice
Shookan feels Scoin is creating their own markets, and says she can’t find actual coin collectors to buy her coins from her. She also says dealers she has approached will only offer her the value of the precious metals they contain.(12:05)
Sound Up Rohini
They have quoted me just the weight, the purchase price for the weight of the gold. And that was completely unacceptable, nowhere near why I paid for the coins.
Voice
While determining the value of any object for sale is certainly guided by what someone is willing to pay for it, our case studies feel Scoin were not entirely honest with them in their dealings.(10:09)
Sound Up Peter
They paint a very pretty picture, but they do not tell you about the cons that you can face.
Sound Up Rohini
I’ve been duped. I’ve been sold an investment that did not materialize.
